prompt.context: Our client is a leading beer manufacturer that has been experiencing stagnant sales in an increasingly competitive industry and is trying to evaluate growth opportunities. A high-level executive has noticed a steady and substantial increase in the consumption of bottled water products. The client is facing increased competition from microbreweries and has already explored ways to penetrate the international market; however, this alone will not enable them to meet their current financial goals. Believing that the assets required to produce bottled water are very similar to those of beer, the client wants to recommend to the CEO that they begin production of bottled water products.
prompt.question: The client has asked our firm to help build the case for why they should enter the bottled water market to achieve their sales and profit goals. First, determine whether the breakeven point seems reasonable. If it is reasonable, how should the client proceed in bringing the product to market?

clarifying_info.q: What is the current size and growth rate of the bottled water market?
clarifying_info.a: Annual growth rate is around 10%. The current market for bottled water is $1.5B in revenue, or 1B bottles.

clarifying_info.q: What is the average selling price per bottle?
clarifying_info.a: Average price per 12oz bottle of water is $1.50.
Water customers are men and women ages 15-65 who lead an active lifestyle. This demographic is growing 5-6% CAGR.

clarifying_info.q: What are the upfront investment and unit costs to enter the market?
clarifying_info.a: Partners require $20M upfront to begin the venture (initial investment cost). Production cost per bottle: $0.50. Distribution cost per bottle: $0.20.

clarifying_info.q: What is the state of the client's production capacity?
clarifying_info.a: Plants are currently running at full capacity producing beer. Building a new facility would cost $50M.

clarifying_info.q: Are there alternative production options besides building a new facility?
clarifying_info.a: Potential partners include soda and juice manufacturers and other beer manufacturers. Due to a decline in sales, two soft drink manufacturers have excess capacity they are willing to outsource. Each could produce 200M bottles per year at a cost under $25M.

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's current financial position?
clarifying_info.a: The client recently acquired a local distributor and has used up much of its cash. It has $25M left. For purposes of this case, assume the client has no access to capital markets to raise additional funds.

clarifying_info.q: What distribution assets does the client have?
clarifying_info.a: The client has one of the industry's most extensive and efficient distribution networks for beer, which overlaps many but not all potential outlets for bottled water.

clarifying_info.q: What is the competitive landscape in bottled water production?
clarifying_info.a: Recent industry analysis suggests that current manufacturing capacity of major water producers will not satisfy domestic demand.

clarifying_info.q: Does the client have marketing capabilities?
clarifying_info.a: The client has recently invested in a new marketing campaign with an outside advertising agency.

exhibits.title: Sample Solution Math
exhibits.shows: A page summarizing the math calculations and overall solution approach for the bottled water market entry case
exhibits.data: Breakeven Point formula: $20M / ($1.50 - $0.50 - $0.20) = 25M units; Total market units: $1.5B / $1.50 = 1B units; Breakeven Market Share: 25M / 1B = 2.5%

framework: Market attractiveness: size, growth rate, demand-supply gap, pricing
Customer analysis: target demographic, preferences, purchase criteria
Competitive landscape: market concentration, capacity constraints, potential responses
Internal capabilities: production capacity, financial position, distribution network, marketing
Profitability / breakeven analysis: upfront investment, unit economics, required market share
Go-to-market approach: build vs. outsource production, distribution strategy, branding
Risks: legislation, execution risk, exit options

questions.prompt: Calculate the breakeven point in units and as a market share percentage.
questions.guidance: A strong answer sets up the breakeven formula correctly: fixed cost divided by contribution margin per unit. Contribution margin = price minus variable costs. Candidate should then express breakeven units as a percentage of total market units to assess feasibility.

math.setup: Fixed cost = $20M (upfront partner investment). Contribution margin per bottle = $1.50 (price) - $0.50 (production) - $0.20 (distribution) = $0.80. Total market units = $1.5B revenue / $1.50 per bottle = 1B bottles.
math.answer: The client needs to sell 25M bottles, representing only 2.5% of the market, to break even on the initial $20M investment.

questions.prompt: Is the breakeven market share of 2.5% achievable? What does the market outlook suggest?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note that 2.5% is a low share target, the market is growing at 10% annually, the target demographic is growing 5-6% CAGR, and current producers cannot meet domestic demand — all supporting a favorable entry case.

questions.prompt: Given that plants are running at full capacity, how should the client produce the bottled water? Evaluate the build-vs-outsource options.
questions.guidance: Candidate should compare two options: (1) Build a new facility at $50M — exceeds the client's $25M cash balance and is not feasible given no access to capital markets. (2) Outsource to soft drink manufacturers with excess capacity — cost under $25M, within budget, each partner can produce up to 200M bottles per year (well above the 25M breakeven), and is lower risk if the client wants to exit later. Outsourcing is the recommended path.

math.setup: Client cash = $25M. New facility cost = $50M. Outsourced capacity cost < $25M per partner.
steps: Outsource option: cost < $25M fits within budget; capacity 200M bottles >> 25M breakeven requirement
math.answer: Outsourcing is the only financially feasible option and provides more than sufficient capacity.

brainstorming.prompt: What areas should the client explore when evaluating this market entry opportunity?

categories.name: Capabilities
ideas: Financial capacity (cash on hand, access to capital)
Production capacity (current utilization, build vs. outsource)
Distribution network strength and coverage overlap

categories.name: Customer
ideas: Willingness to pay for a beer-brand water product

categories.name: Competition
ideas: Market concentration among existing water producers
Potential competitive responses to new entrant

recommendation: Recommend that the client enter the bottled water market by outsourcing production to one of the two soft drink manufacturers with excess capacity.
The client needs only 2.5% market share to break even, the market is growing at 10% annually, and current producers cannot satisfy domestic demand — all pointing to an attractive entry.

Outsourcing costs under $25M (within the client's $25M cash balance), each partner can produce up to 200M bottles per year (well above the 25M breakeven), and the client can leverage its existing extensive distribution network.
This approach is less expensive and less risky than building a $50M facility, and preserves the option to exit if needed.
risks: Client's beer-brand equity may not transfer credibly to bottled water
Distribution network does not cover all potential water retail outlets
Dependence on outsourced partner introduces supply chain and quality risk
Market growth could attract stronger competitors who erode the 2.5% share target
next_steps: Negotiate outsourcing agreement with one or both soft drink manufacturers
Develop a branding and marketing strategy for the bottled water product
Map distribution network gaps and identify partnership or acquisition options to fill them
Set a milestone-based review: reassess after Year 1 to decide whether to continue outsourcing or invest in proprietary capacity
